newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINLAND SHOULD CUT TAXES TO CREATE JOBS -REPORT.
newsitem.headline: FINLAND SHOULD CUT TAXES TO CREATE JOBS -REPORT.

text.p: The Finnish government should cut taxes to reduce unemployment, said a group of senior economists in a report to the economic council on Tuesday.
Income taxes should be cut by about nine billion markka in 1998-99, the report said. Increased economic activity would cover around half of the public sector revenue shortfall.
Big income tax cuts for low-wage earners should pave the way for lower nominal wages for unskilled workers. This would give employers more incentives to hire new staff, the report said.
Earnings-related jobless benefits should be gradually lowered to boost active job hunting by the unemployed, it said.

The economic council is an informal discussion forum led by the prime minister and grouping key cabinet ministers, the central bank governor, trade union and employer confederation leaders and heads of big business lobbies.
The council met on Wednesday morning to review the report requested by Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen last April.
"Lowering the high unemployment is now the most important economic policy goal," the report said.
"A significant and sustained lowering of unemployment is a demanding task," it said, adding success or failure here will be of decisive importance for the public sector finances.
"Public sector spending remains under high pressure and tax revenue low due to mass-unemployment and this makes it more difficult to reduce public indebtedness," the report said.

Strong public sector finances would be important in a possible EMU-environment, it said, adding the policy of halting the increase in state indebtedness must remain on course to ensure that interest rates stay low.
"As a result of a sustained and determined policy state indebtedness is now starting to come to a halt. At the same time real earnings have developed favourably," the economists said.
"The competitiveness is good and the interest rate level has fallen so that the conditions for economic growth are favourable," they said.

"The same kind of consensus and consistency that have been evident in halting state indebtedness and enhancing competitiveness are now needed to implement the structural reforms needed to increase employment," they added.
They underlined that the report's proposals would work towards a substantial upturn in jobs creation only if all measures were implemented -- not just the pleasant ones.
